Around 1007 the Keraites, a Turco-Mongol people of central Mongolia, took up Christianity in the form of the Church of the East, often called the Nestorian church. A Syriac chronicle tells how their khan, lost in a snowstorm, saw a vision of Saint Sergius. The bishop of Merv then wrote to the patriarch in Baghdad asking how a people who lived on meat and milk could keep the Lent fast, and reported some 200,000 baptised.

The Keraites lived along the Tuul and Orkhon rivers and were among the strongest peoples of the steppe in the 1100s. Their khan Toghrul, also called Ong Khan, was first the patron, then the rival, of the young Temüjin, who defeated him in 1203 and became Genghis Khan. Keraite women married into his family: Sorghaghtani Beki, a Christian Keraite, was the mother of Möngke, Hülegü and Kublai.

Their Christian khans are one source of the European legend of Prester John, a priest king in the East who would come to help the crusaders. The conversion shows how far the Church of the East had spread along the Silk Road since it reached Tang China in 635.
